headline: High-risk shared filesystem and git state create prompt-injection, data-leakage, and cascading-error exposure between Gemini CLI and transformers.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Gemini CLI can read/write the filesystem and use MCP, while transformers can read/write files and run browsers. Their shared-state path is via filesystem and git, so attacker-controlled content in one can be consumed by the other as trusted input. This is not provably blocked, but it is not a direct default instruction channel either.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same working directory or git checkout
IF one agent parses files from the shared workspace as instructions or prompts
mitigations: Use separate directories and git remotes for each agent
Disable MCP servers for the Gemini CLI session
Review any file content before feeding it to the other agent
Run one agent at a time when exchanging artifacts
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to shared files

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents can read files in the cwd and write files, and Gemini CLI also has broad network egress plus API calls. If sensitive files are present in the shared workspace, either agent can expose them through outputs or upstream calls. The pair is not documented as isolated, so leakage is plausible in default use.
conditions: IF sensitive documents are placed in the shared workspace
IF Gemini CLI sends workspace-derived content to external APIs
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared directory
Use a redacted staging folder for handoffs
Turn off network access for the Gemini CLI session when handling sensitive files
Restrict file permissions on the workspace
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent workspace isolation

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write and shell execution, and Gemini CLI explicitly shares state with other instances via filesystem and git. Concurrent edits to the same repo can overwrite each other or corrupt git state without locks. The overlap is direct and default-dangerous, so this is high severity.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or repository
IF either agent commits or rebases without external locking
mitigations: Assign separate branches per agent
Pause one agent before the other writes
Use git worktrees for isolation
Check `git status` before each write step
requires-engineering: add file-locking or transaction coordination

D_cascading_error.rationale: Gemini CLI can produce tool-using outputs and transformers can run pipelines or scripts that may act on those outputs. If B treats A's generated text, code, or citations as authoritative, errors can cascade into incorrect documents or executed actions. The pair lacks a built-in verification boundary in the profiles, so the safer severity is high.
conditions: IF transformers consumes Gemini CLI output without a verification step
IF A-generated code or facts are used by B in a downstream pipeline
mitigations: Require human review between agents
Add a validation step before B consumes A's output
Limit A to drafting only, not final instructions
Use schema checks on exchanged artifacts
requires-engineering: implement provenance-aware verification

E_compliance.rationale: No explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented in either profile, so a compliance breach is not established. Gemini CLI handles Google account login optionally and API keys, while transformers is open-source and locally runnable; the main concern is only if regulated data is routed through Gemini's external APIs. The other agent is not cited for a specific compliance gap because none is stated.
conditions: IF regulated data is sent through Gemini CLI's external API calls
IF the deployment requires residency or retention guarantees not documented here
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in Gemini API prompts
Keep transformers local-only for sensitive workloads
Review vendor data-processing terms before use
Log what data leaves the workstation
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for data residency
